questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: An Airworthiness Directive (AD) is —
options: A mandatory instruction to correct an unsafe condition
questions.explain: ADs are legally mandatory actions issued to correct unsafe conditions in a type/product.

questions.q: Responsibility for ensuring an aircraft is in an airworthy condition before flight rests primarily with the —
questions.explain: The PIC must determine the aircraft is airworthy before flight; the owner/operator is responsible for maintenance.

questions.q: Preventive maintenance (e.g. simple servicing) may generally be performed by —
options: A certificated pilot on an aircraft they own/operate (where authorised)
questions.explain: Rules permit certificated pilots to perform listed preventive-maintenance tasks on aircraft they own or operate, within limits.

questions.q: A required instrument or equipment item that is inoperative before flight must be —
options: Handled per the MEL or the applicable inoperative-equipment rule
questions.explain: Inoperative equipment is dispatched per the Minimum Equipment List or the general inoperative-instruments-and-equipment rule.

questions.q: The transponder (and where required altitude reporting) must have been tested/inspected within the preceding —
questions.explain: Transponder and altitude-reporting systems require testing within the preceding 24 calendar months for use in controlled airspace.

questions.q: Continued airworthiness of an aircraft is maintained through —
options: Compliance with the maintenance programme, ADs and inspections
questions.explain: Airworthiness is sustained by the approved maintenance programme, mandatory ADs and required inspections.

questions.q: Supplemental oxygen is required for the flight crew above a cabin pressure altitude of about —
options: A specified altitude for durations/continuous use per the rule (e.g. above ~10,000–12,500 ft)
questions.explain: Rules require crew oxygen above defined cabin altitudes — continuously above the higher threshold and after a time limit at the lower band.

questions.q: An aircraft's Certificate of Airworthiness remains valid provided —
options: The aircraft is maintained and operated within its approved limitations
questions.explain: A C of A stays in effect while the aircraft conforms to type design and is maintained/operated per its limitations and the applicable rules.

questions.q: The document listing an aircraft's operating limitations, markings and placards is the —
options: Approved flight manual / pilot's operating handbook
questions.explain: The AFM/POH contains the certificated limitations, procedures and performance data; required placards echo key limits.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Static wicks fitted to trailing edges serve to —
options: Discharge static electricity to reduce radio interference
questions.explain: Static dischargers (wicks) bleed off accumulated static charge, reducing precipitation-static interference with radios/navaids.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A magneto check before take-off verifies —
options: The ignition system and detects a dead/rough mag
questions.explain: The run-up mag check confirms both ignition systems work and reveals excessive rpm drop from a faulty magneto or fouled plug.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

banks.title: Aviation Weather
banks.desc: Atmosphere, clouds, fronts, thunderstorms, icing and visibility hazards drawn from the FAA Aviation Weather Handbook.

questions.q: What type of cloud is associated with severe turbulence, icing, lightning and hail, and should be avoided?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook identifies cumulonimbus clouds as thunderstorm clouds carrying severe turbulence, icing, lightning and hail - all thunderstorms are hazardous to aircraft.

questions.q: A thunderstorm cell transitions to the mature stage when which event occurs?
options: The downdraft cuts off the moisture supply
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook states a cell transitions to the mature stage when precipitation reaches the surface, creating a strong downdraft alongside the updraft; weather hazards peak toward the end of this stage.

questions.q: In the International Standard Atmosphere, what are the sea level temperature and pressure?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook gives the standard atmosphere as 15 degrees C (59 degrees F) and 29.92 inches of mercury (1013.25 hPa) at sea level.

questions.q: What is the standard temperature lapse rate in the troposphere?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook lists the standard tropospheric lapse rate as 6.5 degrees C per 1,000 metres, which is about 3.57 degrees F - roughly 2 degrees C per 1,000 feet.

questions.q: Which surface weather measurement is most useful for anticipating the formation of fog?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook notes the surface temperature-dewpoint spread is important in anticipating fog; when the spread reaches zero the air is saturated and fog can form.

questions.q: Radiation fog forms primarily under which conditions?
options: Strong winds and overcast skies over water
Clear skies, light winds and moist air over land at night
Warm air moving over a cold sea surface
Air being forced up sloping terrain in daytime
questions.explain: Per the FAA Aviation Weather Handbook, radiation fog is favoured by a shallow moist surface layer, clear skies and light surface winds; it is a nighttime land occurrence caused by terrestrial cooling.

questions.q: How does advection fog form?
options: Moist air moving over a colder surface and cooling below its dewpoint
Nighttime radiational cooling of the ground
Rain evaporating into cold air beneath a front
Air being lifted over a mountain ridge
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook defines advection fog as forming when moist air moves over a colder surface and is cooled below its dewpoint; it is common along coasts and is called sea fog at sea.

questions.q: A microburst is best described as which type of weather hazard?
options: A small-scale, intense downdraft - the most severe type of wind shear
A persistent layer of stratus cloud
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook describes a microburst as a small-scale, intense downdraft that spreads outward at the surface and is the most severe type of wind shear, with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm.

questions.q: Which structural icing type is rough, milky and opaque, and is the most frequently reported icing type?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook describes rime ice as rough, milky and opaque ice formed by instantaneous freezing of small supercooled droplets, and notes it is the most frequently reported icing type.

questions.q: Which force, caused by the Earth's rotation, deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook explains the Coriolis force is an apparent force from the Earth's rotation that deflects air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, acting at a right angle to wind direction.

questions.q: What effect does stable air generally have on the vertical motion of air?
options: It has no effect on vertical motion
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook states atmospheric stability affects vertical motion: stable air suppresses vertical motion, while unstable air enhances it.

questions.q: The arc-shaped leading edge of cool, gusty downdraft air spreading out ahead of a mature thunderstorm is called what?
questions.explain: The FAA Aviation Weather Handbook calls the arc-shaped leading edge of downdraft air a gust front; uplift along it can trigger new cells ahead of the parent cell.

questions.q: A sea breeze typically blows:
options: From land to sea by day
From sea to land by day
questions.explain: By day the land heats faster than the sea, so the surface wind (sea breeze) blows from sea to land.

questions.q: Fog forms when:
options: Air is heated above its dew point
Air is cooled to its dew point
questions.explain: Fog forms when air is cooled to its dew point and water vapour condenses near the surface.

questions.q: Structural icing requires:
options: Visible moisture and a temperature at or below freezing
questions.explain: Airframe icing needs visible moisture and a temperature at or below 0°C.

questions.q: A temperature inversion is a layer in which:
questions.explain: In an inversion, temperature increases with altitude, often trapping haze and stabilising the air.

questions.q: Wind shear is:
options: A sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance
questions.explain: Wind shear is a rapid change in wind velocity over a small change in position, hazardous near the ground.

questions.q: A METAR is:
options: A forecast for the next 24 hours
A routine, observed aviation weather report
questions.explain: A METAR is a routine observation of current conditions at an aerodrome (a TAF is the forecast).

questions.q: A TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) is —
options: A scheduled forecast of expected weather conditions at an aerodrome for a specified period
A record of past observed weather
questions.explain: A TAF is a forecast (not an observation) of expected aerodrome weather over a defined valid period.

questions.q: Convective SIGMETs are issued for hazards including —
options: Severe or embedded thunderstorms and tornadoes
questions.explain: Convective SIGMETs warn of severe convective weather hazards such as severe/embedded thunderstorms, tornadoes, hail and severe turbulence.

questions.q: Katabatic (drainage) winds occur when —
options: Cold, dense air flows downhill under gravity, typically at night
Warm air rises rapidly during the day
questions.explain: Katabatic winds form as cold, denser air drains downslope under gravity, most commonly overnight.

questions.q: Clear-air turbulence (CAT) is most commonly associated with —
options: Strong wind shear near the jet stream
questions.explain: CAT typically occurs in strong wind-shear zones around the jet stream, often without visible cloud to warn pilots.

questions.q: Dew point is best defined as the temperature to which air must be cooled to become —
questions.explain: Dew point is the temperature at which a given parcel of air becomes saturated; the closer the temperature/dew-point spread, the higher the humidity.

questions.q: A warm front is typically associated with —
options: A narrow band of violent thunderstorms
Widespread stratiform cloud and steady precipitation
questions.explain: Warm fronts, with their shallow slope, typically bring extensive stratiform cloud, low ceilings and steady precipitation ahead of the front.

questions.q: The three ingredients required for a thunderstorm to form are moisture, instability and —
questions.explain: Thunderstorms require sufficient moisture, an unstable lapse rate and a lifting force (front, terrain, heating or convergence) to trigger deep convection.

questions.q: Mountain wave turbulence is most likely when strong winds blow —
options: Parallel to a ridge in stable air
Roughly perpendicular to a mountain ridge with a stable layer aloft
questions.explain: Mountain waves form when strong winds cross a ridge roughly perpendicularly with a stable layer aloft, producing wave action, rotors and turbulence downwind.

questions.q: Freezing rain at the surface is a reliable indication of —
options: Warmer air aloft above a sub-freezing surface layer (a temperature inversion)
questions.explain: Freezing rain forms when rain from a warmer layer aloft falls through a sub-freezing surface layer — direct evidence of warmer air above (an inversion).

questions.q: The most hazardous aspect of a microburst for an aircraft on approach is —
options: A rapid shift from a performance-increasing headwind to a performance-decreasing tailwind
questions.explain: Flying through a microburst, the aircraft first meets a headwind (rising performance), then a strong downdraft and finally a tailwind — a sudden loss of airspeed/performance close to the ground.

questions.q: Standard sea-level pressure in the International Standard Atmosphere is —
questions.explain: ISA sea-level pressure is 1013.2 hPa, equal to 29.92 inches of mercury.

questions.q: Which cloud type is a sign of stable air and typically produces steady precipitation?
questions.explain: Stratiform (layered) cloud forms in stable air and yields steady, continuous precipitation; cumuliform cloud signals instability.

questions.q: A halo around the sun or moon, produced by cirrostratus, is often an early sign of —
questions.explain: Cirrostratus and its halo commonly precede an approaching warm front by a day or more.

questions.q: Wind reported by an aviation routine weather report (METAR) is referenced to —
questions.explain: METAR/TAF winds are given in degrees true; ATC-issued surface winds (tower) are magnetic.

questions.q: The dew point is the temperature at which air, cooled at constant pressure, becomes —
questions.explain: Cooling air to its dew point brings it to saturation (100% relative humidity); further cooling causes condensation.

questions.q: Frost on a wing before flight is hazardous because it —
options: Disrupts airflow, reducing lift and increasing stall speed
questions.explain: Even thin frost roughens the wing surface, disrupting the boundary layer — it can reduce lift by a large margin and must be removed before flight.

questions.q: The three stages of an ordinary (air-mass) thunderstorm are cumulus, mature, and —
questions.explain: An air-mass thunderstorm progresses through the cumulus (building), mature (peak, with downdrafts) and dissipating stages.

questions.q: Squall lines are hazardous to aircraft primarily because they —
options: Are easy to fly through between cells
Form a continuous line of thunderstorms often too long to circumnavigate
questions.explain: A squall line is a band of active thunderstorms, often ahead of a cold front, that can be too extensive to safely detour around.

questions.q: A ceiling, in aviation weather, is the height above the surface of the lowest layer reported as —
questions.explain: Ceiling is the AGL height of the lowest broken or overcast layer, or the vertical visibility into an obscuration.

questions.q: Standing lenticular clouds are a visual indication of —
options: Mountain-wave activity and possible severe turbulence
questions.explain: Smooth, lens-shaped standing lenticular clouds mark mountain-wave conditions, with turbulence likely even though the clouds themselves look smooth.

questions.q: For an unsaturated (dry) parcel, the adiabatic lapse rate is approximately —
questions.explain: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 3 °C per 1,000 ft; the average (environmental) lapse rate is about 2 °C per 1,000 ft.

questions.q: Fog that forms as warm, moist air moves over a cooler surface is —
questions.explain: Advection fog forms when warm, moist air is transported horizontally over a colder surface, cooling it to the dew point; unlike radiation fog it needs wind.

questions.q: A trough of low pressure is generally associated with —
questions.explain: Air converges and rises in a trough of low pressure, favouring cloud and unsettled weather; ridges of high pressure favour fair weather.

questions.q: Convective turbulence over land is usually strongest —
options: During the warmest part of the afternoon
questions.explain: Surface heating peaks in the afternoon, driving the strongest thermal (convective) turbulence in the lower atmosphere.

banks.title: Aerodynamics & Aircraft Systems
banks.desc: Forces of flight, stalls, load factor, airspeeds and powerplant systems from the FAA Pilot's Handbook and Airplane Flying Handbook.

questions.q: What are the four forces acting on an aircraft in flight?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge identifies the four forces acting on an aircraft in straight-and-level flight as lift, weight, thrust and drag.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: An aerodynamic stall occurs when which condition is reached?
options: A specific low airspeed is reached
Engine power is reduced to idle
The wing exceeds its critical angle of attack
questions.explain: The FAA Airplane Flying Handbook states a stall occurs when the angle of attack exceeds the wing's critical angle of attack; it can occur at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.

questions.q: Is it possible to exceed the critical angle of attack and stall the wing at high airspeed?
options: No, stalls only occur at low airspeed
Yes, the critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed
Only above maximum structural cruising speed
questions.explain: The FAA Airplane Flying Handbook explicitly states it is possible to exceed the critical angle of attack - and therefore stall - at any airspeed, at any attitude and at any power setting.

questions.q: On a standard airspeed indicator, the lower limit of the white arc represents which airspeed?
options: The power-off stall speed in the landing configuration (VS0)
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states the lower limit of the white arc is VS0 - the stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration with gear and flaps down.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: What does the red line on a standard airspeed indicator indicate?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states the red line marks VNE, the never-exceed speed; operating above it is prohibited as it may cause structural damage or failure.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The yellow arc on an airspeed indicator represents which range?
options: The caution range, to be used only in smooth air
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge describes the yellow arc as the caution range, to be flown within only in smooth air and then only with caution.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Design maneuvering speed (VA) is best described as which of the following?
options: The maximum speed at which the design's limit load can be imposed without structural damage
The best speed for climbing over an obstacle
The maximum speed with flaps extended
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge defines VA as the maximum speed at which the structural design's limit load can be imposed - by gusts or full control deflection - without causing structural damage; it decreases with lighter weight.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Carburetor ice is most likely to form under which conditions?
options: Only in sub-freezing outside air temperatures
Temperatures below 21 degrees C (70 degrees F) with relative humidity above 80 percent
High temperatures with very dry air
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states carburetor ice is most likely when temperatures are below 70 degrees F (21 degrees C) and relative humidity is above 80 percent, though it can occur even at higher temperatures.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Adverse yaw causes an aircraft to yaw in which direction during a turn entry?
options: In the same direction as the bank
Opposite to the direction of the bank
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains adverse yaw results from extra drag on the rising (outside) wing, so from the pilot's perspective the yaw is opposite the direction of the bank.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: How does an increased load factor affect an aircraft's stalling speed?
options: It has no effect on stalling speed
An increased load factor raises the stalling speed
An increased load factor lowers the stalling speed
It only affects stalling speed below 1g
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge discusses load factors and stalling speeds: increasing load factor, such as in a steep turn, increases the speed at which the wing stalls.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: For a given calibrated airspeed, how does true airspeed behave as altitude increases?
options: True airspeed decreases as altitude increases
True airspeed stays the same at all altitudes
True airspeed increases as altitude increases
True airspeed equals groundspeed at all altitudes
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states that because air density decreases with altitude, for a given calibrated airspeed the true airspeed increases as altitude increases.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: In a spark-ignition reciprocating engine, what is the function of the magnetos?
options: To provide the spark that ignites the fuel-air mixture
To meter air into the carburetor
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains the ignition system uses magnetos, spark plugs and leads to provide the spark that ignites the fuel-air mixture in the cylinders.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Aerodynamic lift acts:
questions.explain: Lift acts perpendicular to the relative airflow; drag acts parallel to it.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Induced drag is greatest:
options: At low speed and high angle of attack
questions.explain: Induced drag rises as angle of attack increases, so it is greatest at low speed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: An aeroplane stalls when it exceeds:
questions.explain: A stall is caused by exceeding the critical angle of attack, and can occur at any airspeed or attitude.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: In a level turn, load factor:
questions.explain: As bank angle increases in a level turn, load factor (and stall speed) increases.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Ground effect causes:
options: Increased induced drag near the surface
Reduced induced drag near the surface
questions.explain: Within about one wingspan of the surface, induced drag is reduced, which can cause floating in the flare.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: As aircraft weight decreases, manoeuvring speed (Va):
questions.explain: Va decreases as weight decreases, because a lighter aircraft reaches limiting load factor at a lower speed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: An aircraft's center of gravity (CG) location primarily affects —
questions.explain: CG position strongly affects an aircraft's longitudinal (pitch) stability and how it handles/controls.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Adverse yaw during a turn entry is best countered by —
options: Coordinated use of aileron and rudder
questions.explain: Coordinated rudder use alongside aileron input counteracts adverse yaw when entering/exiting a turn.

questions.q: P-factor (asymmetric propeller loading) is most pronounced —
options: At high angles of attack and high power settings
At idle power on the ground
questions.explain: P-factor increases with high angle of attack and high power, contributing to a yawing tendency.

questions.q: Torque effect from engine and propeller rotation tends to roll the aircraft —
options: Opposite to the direction of propeller rotation
In the same direction as propeller rotation
questions.explain: By Newton's third law, engine/propeller torque rolls the airframe opposite to the direction the propeller turns.

questions.q: Increasing the wing angle of attack increases lift until —
options: The speed of sound is reached
The critical (stalling) angle of attack is exceeded
questions.explain: Lift rises with angle of attack up to the critical angle; beyond it the airflow separates and the wing stalls, regardless of airspeed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Wingtip vortices (and the induced drag they represent) are strongest when an aircraft is —
options: Heavy, clean, and slow (high angle of attack)
questions.explain: Induced drag and wingtip vortices are greatest at high angle of attack — heavy, slow, and clean configuration — such as just after take-off or in slow flight.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Raising flaps generally —
options: Increases the stalling speed and reduces lift/drag at a given speed
Has no effect on stall speed
Increases the critical angle of attack
questions.explain: Retracting flaps reduces camber and lift coefficient, raising the stalling speed and reducing drag for a given airspeed.

questions.q: A forward centre-of-gravity position generally makes an aircraft —
options: Less stable and harder to recover from a stall
More longitudinally stable but requiring more elevator/tail download
Faster in cruise with no penalty
questions.explain: A forward CG increases longitudinal stability and stall resistance but requires greater tail download/elevator authority and can raise stall speed and reduce cruise performance.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Load factor in a coordinated level turn is a function of —
questions.explain: In a level, coordinated turn the load factor depends on bank angle (1/cos of the bank), independent of aircraft weight — e.g. about 1.41 g at 45° bank.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Vne (never-exceed speed) is depicted on the airspeed indicator by the —
questions.explain: Vne is marked by the red radial line; the aircraft must never be flown beyond it.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Bernoulli's principle explains that, as air accelerates over the upper wing surface, its —
questions.explain: Faster-moving air over the curved upper surface has lower static pressure, contributing (with downwash/Newtonian reaction) to lift.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the —
questions.explain: Angle of attack is measured between the wing chord line and the relative wind, not the horizon.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Ground effect is most pronounced when the wing is within about —
questions.explain: Ground effect — reduced induced drag from the interrupted wingtip vortices — is significant within roughly one wingspan of the ground.

questions.q: A wing with washout is twisted so the —
options: Wingtip has a lower angle of incidence than the root
questions.explain: Washout gives the tip a lower incidence than the root so the root stalls first, preserving aileron effectiveness into the stall.

questions.q: Increasing flap deflection generally increases —
options: Lift only, with no drag change
Drag only, with no lift change
questions.explain: Extending flaps increases the wing's camber, raising both the lift coefficient and drag for a given airspeed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Total drag is the sum of induced drag and —
questions.explain: Total drag = induced drag (a by-product of lift, dominant at low speed) + parasite drag (form/skin/interference, dominant at high speed).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Best glide speed gives the —
questions.explain: Best glide speed is flown at the maximum lift-to-drag ratio, giving the greatest gliding distance for altitude lost.

questions.q: A stall is caused by exceeding the critical angle of attack, which can occur —
options: At any airspeed and any attitude
questions.explain: A wing stalls whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded — regardless of airspeed, weight or attitude (e.g. an accelerated stall in a steep turn).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Dihedral (upward wing angle) primarily improves —
questions.explain: Wing dihedral gives lateral stability — a sideslip raises the lower wing's effective angle of attack, rolling the aircraft back to level.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A conventional aircraft's static longitudinal stability depends on the CG being —
options: Forward of the centre of pressure/neutral point
questions.explain: For positive static longitudinal stability the CG must lie ahead of the neutral point; an aft CG reduces or eliminates stability.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: During a spin, the aircraft is —
questions.explain: A spin is a stalled, autorotating descent with one wing more deeply stalled than the other; recovery breaks the stall and stops rotation.

questions.q: Load factor is defined as the ratio of —
questions.explain: Load factor (in g) is lift divided by weight; a 60°-bank level turn produces 2 g.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Retreating-blade stall is a limiting factor for —
questions.explain: In a helicopter at high forward speed the retreating blade sees a lower relative airflow and can stall, limiting Vne — an airplane term does not apply.

questions.q: Turning tendencies at high power and low airspeed (torque, P-factor, slipstream, gyroscopic precession) generally yaw a typical single-engine airplane to the —
questions.explain: With a conventional clockwise-turning propeller (viewed from the cockpit), the combined left-turning tendencies yaw the airplane left, requiring right rudder.

banks.title: Human Factors & Aeromedical
banks.desc: Hypoxia, carbon monoxide, spatial disorientation, fatigue and aeronautical decision-making from FAA aeromedical and risk-management references.

questions.q: Oxygen starvation from hypoxia affects which part of the body first?
questions.explain: The FAA Hypoxia brochure states oxygen starvation first affects the brain so judgment is impaired - a pilot may not realise they are in trouble.

questions.q: At 18,000 feet MSL, how does the available oxygen compare with sea level?
options: It is the same as at sea level
There is about half the oxygen of sea level
There is about one-quarter the oxygen of sea level
There is more oxygen than at sea level
questions.explain: The FAA Hypoxia brochure notes that at 18,000 feet MSL the air pressure is half that at sea level, so only half the oxygen is available.

questions.q: If a pilot detects an unusual cabin smell suggesting carbon monoxide, what is an appropriate immediate action?
options: Turn the cabin heat fully off and increase fresh-air ventilation
Increase cabin heat to clear the air
Ignore it and continue the flight
questions.explain: The FAA Carbon Monoxide brochure advises pilots to turn cabin heat fully off, increase fresh-air ventilation to maximum, consider supplemental oxygen, and land as promptly as possible.

questions.q: A 'black-hole approach' visual illusion is most likely to occur in which situation?
options: A daytime approach over a city
A night approach over water or unlit terrain to a lighted runway with no visible horizon
questions.explain: The FAA Spatial Disorientation brochure describes the black-hole approach illusion as occurring on a night final approach over water or unlighted terrain to a lighted runway beyond which the horizon is not visible.

questions.q: If a pilot experiences a visual illusion or spatial disorientation in flight, what is the recommended response?
options: Trust bodily sensations over the instruments
Have confidence in the flight instruments and ignore conflicting bodily signals
Close the eyes briefly to reset perception
questions.explain: The FAA Spatial Disorientation brochure advises pilots to have confidence in their instruments and ignore conflicting bodily signals, noting accidents usually result from indecision to rely on instruments.

questions.q: Which type of photoreceptor in the eye is used for low-light and night vision?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot Vision brochure states rods are used for low light intensity or night vision, while cones handle colour and detail in brighter light.

questions.q: For effective visual scanning to detect other traffic, each eye movement should be limited to roughly what arc, observing each area for at least one second?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot Vision brochure recommends a series of short, regularly-spaced eye movements not exceeding 10 degrees, with each area observed for at least one second to enable detection.

questions.q: Altitude-induced decompression sickness is caused by which mechanism?
options: Nitrogen coming out of solution and forming bubbles in the body
questions.explain: The FAA Altitude-Induced Decompression Sickness brochure explains that with reduced pressure, dissolved nitrogen can come out of solution and form bubbles in the body - the condition known as 'the bends'.

questions.q: Why must a pilot allow sufficient time after SCUBA diving before flying?
options: Excess nitrogen stored in the body can trigger decompression sickness at altitudes as low as 5,000 ft
Diving reduces visual acuity for several days
Flying too soon causes carbon monoxide poisoning
questions.explain: The FAA Altitude-Induced Decompression Sickness brochure warns that if not enough time is allowed to eliminate excess body nitrogen after diving, altitude DCS can occur at altitudes as low as 5,000 ft or less.

questions.q: What does the IMSAFE checklist help a pilot assess?
options: Personal fitness for flight - Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion
questions.explain: The FAA Risk Management Handbook describes IMSAFE as an acronym for Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion, used by a pilot to identify personal hazards before flight.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the five hazardous attitudes identified in the FAA Risk Management Handbook?
questions.explain: The FAA Risk Management Handbook lists five hazardous attitudes: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability ('It won't happen to me'), macho and resignation.

questions.q: The PAVE checklist is used by a pilot for what purpose?
options: Identifying hazards and managing risk before and during a flight
questions.explain: The FAA Risk Management Handbook presents the PAVE checklist as a tool for risk management analysis, helping the pilot identify hazards to decide on the desirability of undertaking or continuing a flight.

questions.q: The first action for a pilot experiencing hypoxia is to:
questions.explain: Hypoxia is treated by supplemental oxygen and descending to a lower altitude.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Hyperventilation is best corrected by:
questions.explain: Hyperventilation (over-breathing) is corrected by consciously slowing the breathing rate.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Spatial disorientation is best overcome by:
options: Trusting and relying on the flight instruments
questions.explain: When disoriented, the pilot should trust the flight instruments rather than bodily sensations.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The "IM SAFE" checklist is used to assess:
options: The pilot’s personal fitness to fly
questions.explain: IM SAFE (Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating) checks the pilot’s fitness to fly.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning in a light aircraft most often comes from:
questions.explain: CO can leak from a cracked exhaust into the cabin-heat system; a CO detector and fresh air are key defences.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Which is one of the five hazardous attitudes in aeronautical decision-making?
questions.explain: The five hazardous attitudes are anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho and resignation.

questions.q: Fatigue impairs pilot performance primarily by —
options: Slowing reaction time and degrading judgment and decision-making
Having no measurable effect on flying
questions.explain: Fatigue degrades reaction time, attention, and judgment — all critical to safe flying.

questions.q: The FAA's "DECIDE" model for in-flight decision making includes the steps —
options: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
See, Avoid, Report, Log, Wait, Act
Radio, First, Fly, Navigate, Communicate, Land
Aviate, Navigate, Communicate, Stop, Turn, Hold
questions.explain: The DECIDE model structures in-flight decision making as Detect, Estimate, Choose a course of action, Identify solutions, Do the necessary actions, and Evaluate the effect.

questions.q: "Get-there-itis" describes a hazardous mindset in which a pilot —
options: Fixates on completing the flight as planned despite worsening conditions
Refuses to fly under any circumstances
questions.explain: "Get-there-itis" is the hazardous tendency to press on toward the destination despite deteriorating conditions or mounting risk.

questions.q: Situational awareness in flight refers to a pilot's —
options: Accurate perception of the aircraft, environment and their interaction, now and in the near future
Knowledge of the aircraft's paint scheme
Ability to fly without looking outside
questions.explain: Situational awareness is the pilot's accurate, up-to-date mental picture of the aircraft, environment, and how they're likely to evolve.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Empty-field (or 'empty-sky') myopia causes the eyes at high altitude with nothing to focus on to —
options: Relax to a short focal distance, reducing ability to detect distant traffic
questions.explain: With no visual cues the eyes relax to a resting focus of only a few metres, so distant traffic can go undetected — pilots should deliberately focus on distant objects.
questions.cite: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual / aeromedical references

questions.q: The greatest risk from mild hypoxia is that the affected pilot —
options: May feel a false sense of well-being (euphoria) and not recognise the impairment
questions.explain: Insidious hypoxia often produces euphoria and impaired judgement without the pilot recognising the degradation — which is what makes it dangerous.

questions.q: Time of useful consciousness at a cabin altitude of 25,000 ft is on the order of —
questions.explain: At around 25,000 ft, time of useful consciousness after a loss of pressurisation is only about 3–5 minutes, decreasing sharply with altitude.

questions.q: The leans, a common form of vestibular spatial disorientation, is best countered by —
options: Trusting and flying by the flight instruments
questions.explain: The 'leans' is a false sensation of bank; the remedy is to believe and fly the instruments rather than bodily sensations.
questions.cite: FAA Instrument Flying Handbook / aeromedical references

questions.q: The startle/surprise response is a human-factors hazard because it can —
options: Momentarily degrade a pilot's cognitive performance and delay a correct response
questions.explain: A sudden, unexpected event can trigger a startle response that briefly impairs perception and decision-making, delaying an appropriate reaction.

questions.q: Effective crew/single-pilot resource management primarily aims to improve —
options: The management of all available resources — information, equipment and people — to reduce error
questions.explain: Resource management (CRM/SRM) is about using all available resources — information, automation, people and self — to improve situational awareness and decision-making.

questions.q: Hypoxia caused by reduced oxygen partial pressure at altitude is —
questions.explain: Hypoxic (altitude) hypoxia results from the falling partial pressure of oxygen as altitude increases.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning is best described as which type of hypoxia?
questions.explain: CO binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity — anemic (hypemic) hypoxia.

questions.q: Hyperventilation and hypoxia can feel similar; if in doubt at altitude the pilot should —
options: Assume hypoxia and use supplemental oxygen
questions.explain: Because the symptoms overlap and hypoxia is more immediately dangerous, treat the situation as hypoxia — use oxygen and slow the breathing rate.

questions.q: The false climb sensation after a rapid acceleration on take-off is the —
questions.explain: Forward acceleration is sensed as a nose-up (pitch) attitude — the somatogravic illusion — which can prompt a dangerous nose-down input at night/IMC.

questions.q: Staring at a single stationary light at night can make it appear to move — this illusion is —
questions.explain: Autokinesis: a fixed light stared at for several seconds appears to wander; scanning avoids it.

questions.q: The rods of the eye, used for night vision, are —
options: Most sensitive off-centre, so off-centre viewing is used at night
questions.explain: Rods surround the fovea; at night, looking slightly off-centre (off-centre viewing) places images on the more light-sensitive rods.

questions.q: Full dark adaptation of the eyes takes approximately —
questions.explain: Dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes and can be undone quickly by bright white light.

questions.q: A pilot should not fly for at least the recommended time after donating blood or with a recent illness because of —
options: Reduced tolerance to hypoxia and impaired performance
questions.explain: Blood donation, illness, dehydration and similar factors reduce hypoxia tolerance and degrade performance — captured by the 'IM SAFE' checklist.

questions.q: The hazardous attitude 'invulnerability' is countered by the antidote —
questions.explain: 'Invulnerability' ('it won't happen to me') is countered by 'it could happen to me.'

questions.q: Scanning for traffic is most effective using —
options: A series of short, regularly spaced eye movements
questions.explain: Effective scanning uses a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements, each holding briefly, because the eye detects movement/detail only when relatively still.

questions.q: Spatial disorientation is most effectively prevented by —
options: Relying on and believing the flight instruments
questions.explain: In reduced visual reference the vestibular senses mislead; the remedy is to trust the instruments.

questions.q: Middle-ear or sinus block (barotrauma) on descent is best relieved by —
options: Climbing and using the Valsalva/swallowing techniques
questions.explain: If pressure won't equalise on descent, a climb reduces the differential; swallowing, yawning or a gentle Valsalva helps clear the ears/sinuses.

questions.q: 'Get-there-itis' (plan continuation bias) is the tendency to —
options: Continue an original plan despite changing conditions that warrant a diversion
questions.explain: Plan-continuation bias pushes a pilot to press on with the original plan when deteriorating conditions call for a diversion or delay.

questions.q: The 'DECIDE' model and the 3-P (Perceive-Process-Perform) process are tools for —
questions.explain: Both are structured aeronautical decision-making frameworks for identifying and managing risk in flight.

banks.title: Navigation & Flight Planning
banks.desc: Charts, the coordinate system, magnetic variation and deviation, VOR navigation and wind correction from the FAA Pilot's Handbook.

questions.q: Lines running east and west, parallel to the equator and used to measure position north or south, are called what?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states circles parallel to the equator are parallels of latitude, used to measure degrees of latitude north or south of the equator.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: From which location is longitude measured as the zero (Prime) meridian?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states the Prime Meridian, which passes through Greenwich, England, is the zero line from which longitude is measured east and west to 180 degrees.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: In aerial navigation, what is the angular difference between true direction and magnetic direction called?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states the difference between true and magnetic directions is called variation; isogonic lines join points of equal variation.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A line along which there is zero magnetic variation is known as what?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains that along the agonic line the two poles are aligned and there is no variation.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Compass deviation is an error caused by what?
options: The difference between true and magnetic north
The aircraft's own localised magnetic influences acting on the compass
Wind drifting the aircraft off course
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states each aircraft has internal magnetic influences affecting its compass; deviation is corrected using a compass deviation card to obtain the compass course.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Navigating by reference to visible landmarks on the ground is known as what?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge defines pilotage as navigating by reference to visible landmarks, distinct from dead reckoning and radio navigation.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Dead reckoning is best described as which method of navigation?
options: Computing direction and distance from a known position
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge defines dead reckoning as navigation by computations of direction and distance from a known position.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A VOR ground station projects courses outward in all directions; these courses are referred to as what?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains a VOR projects straight-line courses called radials in all directions, identified by numbers from 001 to 360 and referenced to magnetic north.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Because VOR transmits on VHF, its signal reception is subject to what limitation?
options: It is restricted to line-of-sight, so range varies with altitude
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge notes VOR signals are VHF and therefore subject to line-of-sight restrictions, so reception range varies in direct proportion to the aircraft's altitude.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The wind correction angle is applied to do what?
options: Counteract wind drift so the aircraft's track matches the desired course
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge explains the wind correction angle is the number of degrees the heading is offset from the true course to counteract wind drift and keep the track on the desired course.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: What is the scale of a standard sectional aeronautical chart?
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge states sectional charts have a scale of 1:500,000 (1 inch = about 6.86 NM), allowing detailed information to be shown.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Groundspeed differs from true airspeed in what way?
options: Groundspeed is true airspeed adjusted for wind
Groundspeed is always higher than true airspeed
Groundspeed is true airspeed corrected for temperature
Groundspeed and true airspeed are always equal
questions.explain: The FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge defines groundspeed as the actual speed over the ground - true airspeed adjusted for wind; it decreases with a headwind and increases with a tailwind.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Magnetic variation is the angle between:
questions.explain: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north at a location.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Compass deviation is caused by:
questions.explain: Deviation is the compass error produced by the aircraft’s own electrical and metallic components.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: One degree of latitude equals approximately:
questions.explain: One degree of latitude is about 60 nautical miles (1 minute ≈ 1 NM).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A VOR provides the pilot with:
questions.explain: A VOR gives bearing information as radials from the station; DME adds distance.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Isogonic lines on a chart connect points of equal:
questions.explain: Isogonic lines join points of equal magnetic variation (an agonic line has zero variation).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Dead-reckoning navigation estimates position using:
questions.explain: Dead reckoning computes position from a known start using heading, speed, wind and elapsed time.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A great circle route between two points represents —
options: The shortest distance between them along the Earth's surface
questions.explain: A great circle is the shortest path between two points on a sphere; a rhumb line (constant heading) is usually longer.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) provides the pilot with —
questions.explain: DME gives slant-range distance from the aircraft to the ground station, often paired with a VOR for bearing.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: An ADF (Automatic Direction Finder) needle points toward —
options: The tuned NDB station, regardless of aircraft heading
questions.explain: An ADF needle points at the tuned NDB station's relative bearing, independent of the aircraft's heading reference.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The variation in compass reading caused by an aircraft's own magnetic and electrical equipment is corrected for using a —
questions.explain: A compass deviation card, mounted near the compass, lists correction values for the aircraft's own magnetic interference at various headings.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A rhumb line (loxodrome) is a track that —
options: Crosses every meridian at the same angle and appears straight on a Mercator chart
Is the shortest distance between two points
questions.explain: A rhumb line maintains a constant true bearing, crossing all meridians at the same angle; it plots as a straight line on a Mercator projection but is not the shortest route.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: To convert a true heading to a magnetic heading, a pilot applies —
questions.explain: Magnetic variation (the angle between true and magnetic north) is applied to convert true to magnetic; deviation is then applied to obtain compass heading.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: On a sectional chart the effect of 'east is least, west is best' is a memory aid for applying —
options: Variation between true and magnetic (subtract easterly, add westerly to true)
questions.explain: 'East is least (subtract), west is best (add)' reminds pilots to subtract easterly and add westerly variation when converting a true course to a magnetic course.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A VOR radial is defined as a magnetic bearing —
questions.explain: A radial is a magnetic course oriented FROM the VOR station; the aircraft is on a given radial regardless of which way it is heading.

questions.q: An RNAV/GNSS system computes position primarily from —
questions.explain: A GNSS receiver derives three-dimensional position from the ranging signals of several satellites simultaneously.

questions.q: Given a true airspeed of 100 kt and a direct 20 kt tailwind, the groundspeed is —
questions.explain: A direct tailwind adds to true airspeed: 100 kt TAS + 20 kt tailwind = 120 kt groundspeed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: On a Lambert conformal / sectional chart, a straight line most nearly represents a —
questions.explain: On the Lambert conformal conic projection used for sectionals, a straight line approximates a great circle — the shortest route.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: True airspeed compared with calibrated airspeed, at altitude, is generally —
questions.explain: As altitude increases and air density falls, true airspeed exceeds calibrated (indicated) airspeed for the same dynamic pressure.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A VOR receiver check using a designated VOT should read —
questions.explain: Over a VOT the CDI centres on 0° with a FROM indication (or 180° TO), within a ±4° tolerance.

questions.q: The maximum reception range of a VOR is limited chiefly by —
questions.explain: VOR is VHF and line-of-sight, so reception range increases with altitude and is blocked by terrain.

questions.q: An ADF needle points to the station; to track TO an NDB the pilot uses —
options: Relative bearing plus magnetic heading = magnetic bearing to the station
questions.explain: Magnetic bearing to the station = magnetic heading + relative bearing (the angle from the nose to the needle).

questions.q: Isogonic lines on an aeronautical chart connect points of equal —
questions.explain: Isogonic lines join points of equal magnetic variation; the agonic line is where variation is zero.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: One nautical mile corresponds to approximately —
options: One minute of longitude at all latitudes
questions.explain: One nautical mile ≈ one minute of arc of latitude (about 1.15 statute miles / 1.852 km).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Wind correction angle is applied so that the aircraft's —
options: Heading differs from track to offset drift
questions.explain: The pilot crabs into wind — heading offset from the desired track — so drift is cancelled and the track is maintained.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: RAIM, associated with GPS/GNSS navigation, provides —
options: Integrity monitoring of the satellite solution
questions.explain: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring cross-checks redundant satellite signals and warns the pilot if the position solution is unreliable.

questions.q: A pilotage cross-check compares —
options: Only the compass with the DG
questions.explain: Pilotage is navigation by visual reference to landmarks, cross-checked against the chart.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: DME slant-range error is greatest when the aircraft is —
options: Far from and low over the station
Close to and high over the station
On the ground at the station
questions.explain: DME measures slant range; the difference from ground distance is largest when directly over the station at altitude and negligible far away.

questions.q: Magnetic deviation is corrected by reference to the aircraft's —
questions.explain: Deviation — compass error from the aircraft's own magnetic fields — is listed on the compass correction card for various headings.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A course line drawn on a chart and measured against a meridian gives the —
questions.explain: Measuring the plotted line against a meridian yields true course; applying variation gives magnetic course, then deviation gives compass course.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: When flying from an area of high pressure/temperature into low without resetting the altimeter, the true altitude will be —
questions.explain: 'From high to low, look out below' — flying into lower pressure or colder air makes true altitude lower than the altimeter indicates.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

banks.title: Flight Planning & Fuel
banks.desc: Mass & balance, fuel reserves, performance and the ISA — the planning numbers.
banks.source: GACAR Part 91 · FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: On a standard day (ISA), what is the sea-level temperature?
questions.explain: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere defines sea level as 15°C and 1013.25 hPa.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: What is the approximate ISA temperature lapse rate in the troposphere?
questions.explain: Temperature falls about 2°C (1.98°C) per 1,000 ft up to the tropopause.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: How does a high density altitude affect take-off performance?
questions.explain: Thinner air reduces engine thrust and lift, lengthening the take-off roll and flattening the climb.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Loading an aircraft aft of its centre-of-gravity limit mainly affects what?
questions.explain: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can make stall recovery difficult.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Final reserve fuel is best described as fuel that…
options: may be used during the cruise
should never be planned for use
questions.explain: Final reserve is a protected minimum on landing — it is never planned to be consumed en route.

questions.q: One nautical mile is approximately how many metres?
questions.explain: By definition 1 NM = 1,852 m (1,609 m is a statute mile).
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: With a true airspeed of 120 kt and a 20 kt direct headwind, the groundspeed is…
questions.explain: A headwind subtracts from TAS: 120 − 20 = 100 kt groundspeed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: To convert a fuel volume in litres to a mass, you multiply by its…
questions.explain: Mass = volume × density. Avgas density is roughly 0.72 kg/L.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A stronger headwind component has what effect on take-off and landing distance?
questions.explain: A headwind reduces the ground run required for both take-off and landing.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Density altitude equals pressure altitude when…
options: the temperature equals ISA for that level
questions.explain: When the actual temperature matches the ISA value for that level, density altitude equals pressure altitude.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Pressure altitude is the altitude read when the altimeter sub-scale is set to:
questions.explain: Pressure altitude is indicated when the altimeter is set to the standard 1013.25 hPa / 29.92 inHg.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The crosswind component is greatest when the wind is:
questions.explain: A wind at 90° to the runway is entirely crosswind; aligned with the runway it is all headwind.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Increasing aircraft weight will:
questions.explain: Greater weight increases both take-off and landing distance and raises the stall speed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: On a hot, high-elevation aerodrome, density altitude is:
questions.explain: High temperature raises density altitude above pressure altitude, degrading performance.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A VFR flight must plan to carry fuel to the destination plus:
questions.explain: Fuel planning must include trip fuel plus the required reserves under GACAR Part 91.

questions.q: Contingency (or extra) fuel is carried to allow for:
options: Unforeseen factors such as wind or re-routing
questions.explain: Contingency fuel covers unforeseen deviations from the plan, such as stronger winds or re-routing.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: For a fixed indicated airspeed, true airspeed:
questions.explain: As air density falls with altitude, true airspeed is higher than indicated airspeed for the same IAS.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A wind correction angle is applied to the:
options: Heading, to maintain the desired track
questions.explain: The pilot turns the heading into wind by the wind correction angle to track the desired course.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The E6B flight computer (mechanical or electronic) is primarily used to calculate —
options: Time, speed, distance, fuel and wind-related values for flight planning
questions.explain: The E6B is a flight-planning calculator for time/speed/distance, fuel, and wind-triangle problems.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Weight and balance calculations before flight ensure the aircraft is operated —
options: Within its certificated weight and center-of-gravity limits
questions.explain: Pre-flight weight and balance planning keeps the aircraft within its certificated weight and CG envelope for safe handling.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A NOTAM should be checked during flight planning because it may report —
options: Temporary hazards or changes such as runway closures or navaid outages
questions.explain: Preflight action requires familiarity with all available information, and NOTAMs carry time-critical changes (closures, outages, hazards) not yet reflected on charts.

questions.q: "Top of descent" in flight planning is the point calculated so the aircraft —
options: Reaches the desired altitude/position at the planned descent rate
Always occurs directly over the destination airport
questions.explain: Top-of-descent planning uses a target descent rate/gradient so the aircraft reaches the desired point and altitude at the right time.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for —
questions.explain: Density altitude = pressure altitude corrected for temperature deviation from ISA; high density altitude degrades performance.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: On a high, hot, humid day, take-off and climb performance will —
questions.explain: High density altitude reduces engine power, propeller thrust and lift, lengthening the take-off roll and reducing climb.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The weight beyond which an aircraft may not be loaded for flight is the —
questions.explain: The maximum certificated gross weight is a structural/performance limit that must not be exceeded.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Loading an aircraft aft of the rearward CG limit tends to make it —
options: More stable and easy to recover from a stall
Less stable and harder to recover from a stall/spin
questions.explain: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can make stall/spin recovery difficult or impossible.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: If total weight is unchanged but the CG moves forward, the aircraft generally becomes —
options: More stable but with a higher stall speed and more elevator force needed
questions.explain: A forward CG increases stability and stall speed and requires more elevator/tail download — cruise performance drops slightly.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Fuel required for a flight, in planning, must include taxi, trip, contingency, alternate, and —
questions.explain: Standard fuel planning adds a final reserve on top of taxi, trip, contingency and alternate fuel.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: With a true airspeed of 100 kt and a 25 kt direct headwind, groundspeed is —
questions.explain: A direct headwind subtracts from TAS: 100 − 25 = 75 kt groundspeed.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Given 90 kt groundspeed, how long to cover 30 NM?
questions.explain: Time = distance/speed = 30 NM ÷ 90 kt = 1/3 hour = 20 minutes.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A crosswind component is largest when the wind is —
questions.explain: The crosswind component is the wind speed times the sine of the angle to the runway — maximal at 90°.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A standard-rate turn is a turn at —
questions.explain: A standard-rate (rate-one) turn is 3° per second, completing a 360° turn in two minutes.

questions.q: To convert litres of avgas to a weight, a pilot multiplies by the fuel's —
questions.explain: Volume × density (specific gravity ≈ 0.72 for avgas) gives fuel weight, needed for weight-and-balance.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: A NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) informs pilots of —
options: Time-critical aeronautical information such as closures and outages
questions.explain: NOTAMs give timely notice of hazards or changes — runway/taxiway closures, navaid outages, temporary restrictions — essential in pre-flight planning.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: Extra (contingency) fuel is carried to cover —
options: Unforeseen factors such as routing changes, wind or ATC delays
Nothing — it is optional and never planned
questions.explain: Contingency fuel is a margin for the unexpected — adverse winds, re-routes, holding — beyond the planned trip and reserves.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge

questions.q: The point in a flight plan beyond which it is quicker to continue than to return is the —
options: Point of no return / equal-time point concept
questions.explain: The equal-time point (or point of no return, fuel-based) is where continuing and returning take the same time/fuel — key for long over-water or remote legs.
questions.cite: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge
